title: Built an app where AI agents paper trade and explain their trades
author: TheiaFintech
selftext:
Been working on this for a while and wanted to share.

It's an iOS app called Theia. A handful of AI agents research the market every day, and each one runs its own paper portfolio.

How it works:

* 5 research agents each cover one area: prediction markets (Kalshi/Polymarket), insider and congress trades, valuation, quant signals, and missed opportunities
* A portfolio manager agent reads their research and makes the trades
* Strategy agents each follow their own thesis, and you can make your own in plain English

They use live quotes, earnings data, insider filings, DCF, treasury rates, fundamentals on about 6k US stocks, and web/news search.

It runs once a day, so it fits swing trading or long-term investing, not day trading.

You can also chat with any agent and ask why it made a trade. It answers from its actual trades and research.

Paper trading only for now. It's free to use, but if you want extra usage and more agents, DM me for a promo code.

[Theia (iOS)](https://apps.apple.com/app/apple-store/id6738607499?pt=123782442&ct=RedditAIAgentAd1&mt=8)

I'd love feedback.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
disclosure up front: Quantradin is mine, I built it, and it sits in the same corner (paper portfolios, strategies written in plain English), so read this as a competitor being nosy rather than a review.

the once-a-day cadence is a real choice and I think a good one for agents that read filings and news. what decides whether the paper numbers mean anything is the fill: when the manager agent buys, does it get the quote at research time or the next open? if it's the research-time quote, a swing bot looks better than it will ever be live.

the chat-with-the-agent-about-its-own-trade feature is what I'd copy first. most tools show you the trade and not the reasoning, and the reasoning is where you catch a bad thesis early.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Letting users ask why a trade was made is useful, but the answer should come from a log written at the time of the trade (inputs, timestamp, reason), not reconstructed afterward, or the explanations can drift. I'd show each agent's record against SPY with the trade count and costs, plus a plain "no trade" count, since a daily agent over a few weeks will look good or bad mostly by luck. Earnings and macro dates matter a lot for a once-a-day swing system, and Cymetica's EventTrader (event timing for earnings and macro releases) is one source for that.
